title: Liverpool fans turn Anfield crowd yellow with protest against rising ticket prices
content:
Thousands of Liverpool supporters held up yellow cards in protest at planned ticket price increases during their Premier League clash with Crystal Palace on Saturday.

All four sides of Anfield took part in the next phase of the campaign organised by supporters’ groups as the chant of “you greedy b—-rds, enough is enough” rang out around the stadium.

It was aimed at American owners Fenway Sports Group (FSG), who last month announced plans to increase ticket prices by three per cent for next season with further inflation-linked rises to come in 2027-28 and 2028-29.

Prior to the Palace game, the club’s Supporters’ Board called on fans “to make themselves heard” as they urged to FSG to reconsider the price hike.

The 13th minute was selected for the protest because Liverpool’s inflation-linked rises, capped at a maximum of five per cent per season for 2027-28 and 2028-29, mean that ticket prices could in theory rise by a maximum of 13 per cent over the next three years.

Senior Anfield officials insist that current forecasts suggest a 2.3 per cent rise for 2027-28 and then two per cent in 2028-29, equalling a three-year impact of 7.3 per cent rather than 13 per cent.

Under those projections, adult general admission ticket prices would rise between £3 and £4.50 per person per game over the next three years, while adult season tickets would increase by no more than £3.50 per game for season ticket holders across the same period.

A total of 75,00 yellow cards were printed and distributed to fans around the stadium and in surrounding pubs and cafes. The protest was backed by a number of supporters’ groups including Spirit of Shankly, Spion Kop 1906, Kop Outs (the LGBTQ+ supporters’ group), cultuRED (faith and ethnicity supporters’ group), LFC Women’s Supporters Club, and multiple branches of the Official Liverpool Supporters’ Club.

It marked the next phase in the campaign after flags and banners were withdrawn from the Kop. Supporters’ groups also launched the ‘Not A Pound In The Ground’ initiative, which urges fans not to spend money inside Anfield, and have taken out street advertising across the city.

Liverpool CEO Billy Hogan recently wrote to all season ticket holders and members in which he pointed to the club’s rising costs as the reason behind the price increases.

“No one at Liverpool Football Club takes decisions on ticket pricing lightly,” he said.

“Our matchday operating costs at Anfield have risen significantly in recent years — up 85 per cent including Anfield Road (or 57 per cent excluding Anfield Road) over the past decade, with utility costs up 107 per cent over just the past four years and business rates up 286 per cent in that same period. Over the last decade, we have increased ticket prices by just four per cent to keep any rise in ticket prices to a minimum.

“Against that backdrop, we believe linking any increases to inflation, confirmed as a three per cent rise for the 2026-27 season, is the fairest and most transparent way to attempt to cover some of those uncontrollable costs.”
